No Result View All Result Home News Politics Business Sport Football Health Entertainment Education Opinion Editorial Columns Others LeVogue Magazine Conferences National Economy Contact Us Hausa Edition Home News Politics Business Sport Football Health Entertainment Education Opinion Editorial Columns Others LeVogue Magazine Conferences National Economy Contact Us No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Politicians Who Have Contested Nigeria’s Presidency More Than Once Since 1999 by Oyindamola Olawuyi 3 seconds ago in Feature Share on WhatsApp Share on Facebook Share on X Telegram Since Nigeria returned to democratic rule in 1999, several politicians have contested the country’s presidential elections more than once, seeking to lead Africa’s most populous nation.
While some eventually achieved their ambition after multiple attempts, others remained unsuccessful despite participating in successive election cycles.
From former President Muhammadu Buhari, who contested five consecutive presidential elections, to former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar, who appeared on the ballot three times, here are 12 politicians who have contested Nigeria’s presidency more than once since 1999.
Former President Olusegun Obasanjo contested Nigeria’s presidential elections in 1999 and 2003 under the platform of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP).
In 1999, he defeated Olu Falae, the joint presidential candidate of the Alliance for Democracy (AD) and All People’s Party (APP), to emerge as president following the country’s return to civilian rule.
He secured re-election in 2003, defeating several challengers, including Muhammadu Buhari of the All Nigeria People’s Party (ANPP) and Chukwuemeka Odumegwu-Ojukwu of the All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA).
Obasanjo completed his second term in 2007 after serving as president for eight years.
Former President Muhammadu Buhari contested five consecutive presidential elections between 2003 and 2019.
His first attempt was in 2003 under the ANPP, when he lost to incumbent President Olusegun Obasanjo. He returned in 2007 under the same party but lost to Umaru Musa Yar’Adua.
In 2011, Buhari contested under the Congress for Progressive Change (CPC), losing to Goodluck Jonathan of the PDP.
He eventually won the presidency in 2015 under the All Progressives Congress (APC), defeating incumbent President Jonathan in an election that marked the first time an opposition party defeated a sitting president at the polls.
Buhari secured re-election in 2019, defeating Atiku Abubakar of the PDP.
Former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar contested Nigeria’s presidential elections in 2007, 2019 and 2023.
His first appearance on the presidential ballot was in 2007, when he contested under the Action Congress (AC) after leaving the PDP. He finished third behind Umaru Musa Yar’Adua and Muhammadu Buhari.
Atiku returned in 2019 as the PDP’s presidential candidate but lost to incumbent President Buhari.
In 2023, he again secured the PDP presidential ticket and contested against Bola Tinubu of the APC, Peter Obi of the Labour Party (LP) and Rabiu Kwankwaso of the New Nigeria Peoples Party (NNPP).
He finished second behind Tinubu, who was declared winner of the election.
Former President Goodluck Jonathan contested Nigeria’s presidential elections in 2011 and 2015 under the PDP.
Although he became acting president in 2010 following the death of President Umaru Musa Yar’Adua, Jonathan first contested a presidential election in 2011. He won, defeating candidates including Muhammadu Buhari of the CPC and Nuhu Ribadu of the Action Congress of Nigeria (ACN).
He secured the PDP’s ticket again in 2015 but lost to Buhari, who contested under the APC.
Jonathan subsequently conceded defeat and congratulated Buhari, becoming the first sitting Nigerian president to lose a re-election bid at the polls.
Former Biafran leader Chukwuemeka Odumegwu-Ojukwu contested Nigeria’s presidential elections in 2003 and 2007 under APGA.
In 2003, he contested against incumbent President Olusegun Obasanjo and Muhammadu Buhari, among other candidates, but lost to Obasanjo.
He returned to the presidential race in 2007, again representing APGA, but was unsuccessful.
Clergyman and politician Chris Okotie contested Nigeria’s presidential elections in 2003, 2007, 2011 and 2019.
He first contested in 2003 under the Justice Party (JP), after leaving the National Democratic Party (NDP), where he had initially sought its presidential ticket.
He subsequently established the Fresh Democratic Party (FRESH) and contested the 2007, 2011 and 2019 presidential elections under its platform.
Ambrose Owuru contested Nigeria’s presidential elections in 2007, 2011, 2015 and 2019.
He first appeared on the ballot in 2007 under the Hope Democratic Party (HDP) and returned in 2011 under the same party.
In 2015, he contested under the Hope Party, before returning to the presidential race in 2019 under the HDP.
Politician Olapade Agoro contested Nigeria’s presidential elections in 2003 and 2007 under the National Action Council (NAC).
He first appeared on the ballot in 2003, when he contested against incumbent President Olusegun Obasanjo and other candidates.
He returned in 2007 under the same party but was unsuccessful in his bid to become president.
Former presidential candidate Christopher Pere Ajuwa contested Nigeria’s presidential elections in 2003 and 2007.
He first contested in 2003 under the Liberal Democratic Party of Nigeria (LDPN).
In 2007, he returned to the presidential race under the Alliance for Democracy (AD), following the death of the party’s initial presidential candidate, Adebayo Adefarati.
Ajuwa was unsuccessful in both elections. He died on January 31, 2017.
Author and politician Arthur Nwankwo contested Nigeria’s presidential elections in 2003 and 2007 under the People’s Mandate Party (PMP).
He first appeared on the ballot in 2003, when he contested against incumbent President Olusegun Obasanjo and other candidates.
He returned in 2007 under the same party but did not win the election.
Emmanuel Osita Okereke contested Nigeria’s presidential elections in 2003 and 2007.
He first appeared on the ballot in 2003 under the African People’s Liberation Party (APLP).
He returned in 2007 under the African Liberation Party (ALP), but was again unsuccessful in his bid for the presidency.
Mojisola Adekunle-Obasanjo, a retired military officer and politician, contested Nigeria’s presidential elections in 2003 and 2007 under the Masses Movement of Nigeria (MMN).
She first contested in 2003, becoming the only female presidential candidate on the ballot in that election.
She returned in 2007 under the same party but was unsuccessful.
